author: Wang, Liao and Jingrou, Deng and Tao, Li
title: Influencing factors of urban drone delivery choice behavior in the context of the low-altitude economy; [低空经济下城市无人机配送选择行为影响因素研究]
journal: Journal of Shenzhen University Science and Engineering
abstract: Driven by the development of the low-altitude economy, drone delivery has emerged as a new driver for upgrading urban logistics systems. To investigate urban residents' preferences and decision-making mechanisms regarding drone delivery services, this study takes Shenzhen, China, as a case study. Based on random utility theory, revealed preferences (RP) and stated preferences (SP) surveys are conducted, and discrete choice models are employed to examine the effects of key factors on residents' actual choice behavior towards drone delivery services and the associated value conversion. The results show that residents exhibit risk-averse decision-making characteristics, and factors including safety, delivery cost, delivery time, and noise significantly influence the acceptance of drone delivery. Although variables such as gender, residential floor level, and residential location do not show significant main effects, their interaction effects with delivery cost and safety are significant, indicating that individual characteristics affect acceptance through interaction mechanisms. The effects of different factors vary substantially: safety and delivery cost have the greatest impacts on residents' choice behavior, followed by delivery time, while noise has the weakest effect. Furthermore, residents demonstrate different levels of sensitivity to these factors, with scenarios characterized by high safety and low delivery fees being the most attractive. Therefore, improving delivery safety and controlling delivery costs are essential for enhancing public acceptance of drone delivery, while differentiated strategies should be developed according to the distinct characteristics of different population groups. © 2026 Science Press. author: Peng, Yafeng and Zeng, Jinxin and Chen, Hui and Li, Yujun
title: Validation and application of the Chinese version of the abbreviated math anxiety scale
abstract: Background: Evidence on the psychometric performance of the Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale (AMAS) and the heterogeneity of math anxiety among Chinese secondary-school students remains limited. This study evaluated the Chinese version of the AMAS (AMAS-C) and examined latent profiles of math anxiety and their associations with demographic and educational variables. Methods: Participants were 936 secondary-school students from Guangdong and Jiangxi, China. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega. Confirmatory factor analysis, external construct-validity analysis, and item response theory were used to evaluate the scale's measurement properties. Latent profile analysis was conducted on the nine AMAS items, followed by proportional-odds logistic regression. Results: The AMAS-C showed good internal consistency (α = 0.87; ω = 0.89), and its total score was negatively associated with mathematics attitudes (r = −0.57). The bifactor model provided the best fit in both the CFA and IRT comparisons. This model included a dominant general math-anxiety factor and two orthogonal context-specific factors representing residual variation associated with learning and evaluation situations. The test information function showed that the AMAS-C provided adequate measurement precision across a broad range of math-anxiety levels. LPA identified three quantitatively ordered profiles—Low Anxiety Across Both Contexts (24.6%), Intermediate Anxiety with Pronounced Evaluation Anxiety (50.0%), and High Anxiety Across Both Contexts (25.4%). These profiles differed in overall anxiety level and the relative prominence of learning and evaluation anxiety. Gender and mathematics performance were significantly associated with profile membership, whereas school stage, only-child status, and region were not. Female students had higher cumulative odds of belonging to a higher-anxiety profile than male students (OR = 1.70, 95% CI [1.32, 2.19]). Poorer mathematics performance was associated with lower predicted probabilities of first-profile membership and higher probabilities of third-profile membership. The predicted probability of second-profile membership peaked in intermediate performance categories. Conclusions: The AMAS-C demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity evidence among Chinese secondary-school students. Among the candidate models examined, the bifactor model provided a reasonable working representation of the data, with a predominant general math anxiety factor. The IRT results indicated adequate item functioning and useful measurement precision across a range of math anxiety levels. The LPA identified three ordered profiles: Low Anxiety Across Both Contexts, Intermediate Anxiety with Pronounced Evaluation Anxiety, and High Anxiety Across Both Contexts. These profiles differed in overall anxiety level and the relative prominence of learning- and evaluation-related anxiety. Female students and students reporting poorer mathematics performance were more likely to belong to higher-anxiety profiles, whereas school stage, only-child status, and region showed no statistically significant independent associations with profile membership. © 2026 The Authors. author: Huang, Zhefan and Wang, Kaidi and Lu, Bingjie and Wang, Mo and Hill, Aaron D. and Pryor, Christopher
title: Leaving on a High or Low Note? An Achievement Goal Perspective on Executive Retirement
abstract: Executive retirement represents a pivotal career transition with significant implications. However, our understanding of the antecedents of executive retirement remains limited. We contend that, different from the retirement of general employees, it is important to position executive retirement within an achievement context and consider factors such as firm performance and achievement goal orientations. Drawing on late adulthood developmental psychology, we propose an achievement goal framework to theorize the relationship between firm performance and executive retirement, and the moderating roles of goal orientations. We theorize that firm performance is associated with two distinct mechanisms: the legacy fulfillment mechanism (salient for executives with high performance) and the selective prioritization mechanism (salient for executives with low performance), which together result in a U-shaped relationship between firm performance and the likelihood of executive retirement. We further consider executives’ goal orientations as boundary conditions to probe the underlying mechanisms. We found general support for our theory using an archival dataset of 1840 chief executive officers from S&P 1500 firms (Study 1) and a two-wave survey of 363 executives (Study 2). By integrating developmental psychology theories into the executive retirement literature, our research sheds light on executive retirement decisions through a developmental psychology lens. © 2026 The Author(s). author: Njøten, Håkon and Feyer, Frida K.
title: From fragmentation to framework: defining core human competencies for higher education and the workplace
journal: Higher Education, Skills and Work-based Learning
abstract: Purpose – This article addresses the lack of a coherent, shared language for human-centred competencies in higher education, introducing core human competencies (CHCs) and the 4S framework as an integrative alternative to fragmented terminology such as soft skills, transferable skills and 21st-century skills. Design/methodology/approach – A dual-strategy methodology was employed: a synthesis of leading international competency frameworks (CASEL, BESSI, CCR, OECD Learning Compass, 2030) combined with a structured bibliometric analysis of 880 Scopus-indexed publications (2009–2025), using VOSviewer keyword co-occurrence mapping across seven identified clusters. Findings – Fifteen core competencies were identified from frameworks and research clusters. These are organised into the 4S framework: Self-awareness, Self-leadership, Situational management and Social capacities, positioning CHCs as a holistic framework. Research limitations/implications – The framework is conceptual and requires psychometric validation, longitudinal testing and cross-cultural assessment. Future research should examine predictive validity, factor structure and applicability across disciplines and cultural contexts. Practical implications – The 4S framework offers higher education institutions a shared conceptual language for curriculum design, learning outcomes, pedagogy, staff development and institutional strategy. Originality/value – This article provides the first empirically informed synthesis producing a unified taxonomy of CHCs applicable across higher education contexts, reducing terminological redundancy and offering a practically useable developmental architecture. 2026 © Emerald Publishing Limited

author: Fortuna, Paweł
title: Positive Cyberpsychology: Human Flourishing in a Digital Era
journal: Positive Cyberpsychology: Human Flourishing in a Digital Era
abstract: Well-being supported by digital technologies, grounded in research-based frameworks Researchers and practitioners need systematic approaches to studying how technology enhances rather than diminishes human flourishing. Positive Cyberpsychology: Human Flourishing in a Digital Era introduces PCyb as a field examining factors and processes that support well-being in digital interactions. Paweł Fortuna, one of the pioneers in positive cyberpsychology with over 50 peer-reviewed publications, provides the first comprehensive English-language framework for this emerging field. The book integrates and systematizes empirical findings using the psychological models of flourishing across health, relationships, personal growth, education and work contexts. Structured around three guiding questions—Why is PCyb? What is PCyb? How is PCyb?—it traces the field’s disciplinary development, connects positive psychology with cyberpsychology into a coherent integrative framework. Theoretical insights are combined with empirically grounded examples for immediate research application. Readers will also find: A concrete research framework that outlines specific psychological investigations rather than general approaches to technology design In-depth analysis revealing strong connections between positive psychology, cyberpsychology, and design practices for well-being-oriented digital experiences Concepts, directions, and methods for studying digital strengths, digital well-being, positive technology interventions, and the upward dynamics of flourishing in digital contexts. Evidence-informed insights relevant to implementing flourishing-oriented solutions across diverse contexts spanning AI-driven systems, applications, social media platforms, immersive technologies and gaming. Theoretical foundations combined with actionable examples suitable for coursework in cyberpsychology, positive psychology, AI ethics, and design Researchers and students in psychology, cyberpsychology, AI, and digital humanities will find essential and integrative frameworks and a rich source of research directions for advancing well-being-focused technology studies. Technology designers, UX specialists, and educators developing courses in positive psychology or ethical AI will gain research-informed guidance for shaping digital experiences that genuinely support human flourishing. © 2027 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

author: Hausfeld, Mary M. and Hampel, Vera and Bach, Leon J. and Menges, Jochen I.
title: Putting assumptions to the test: A meta-analytic review of gender differences in emotional intelligence and specific emotion abilities.
abstract: Are women more emotionally intelligent than men? Emotional intelligence (EI) is often colloquially ascribed to women, yet the extant empirical literature yields inconclusive results and EI theories are largely oblivious to gender as an explanatory dimension. To re-evaluate the literature, test key moderators, and develop stronger theory on EI, we examine whether and to what extent gender differences manifest in EI through a meta-analytic review of 1,279 articles comprised of 1,428 samples containing 609,278 participants drawn from published and unpublished work until December 31, 2023. The results suggest gender differences in general EI such that women appear to have higher EI on average, as well as more nuanced gender differences across specific emotional abilities, including some where there may be no difference. Women's advantage is stronger for other- than self-focused emotional abilities and varies by measurement type, with smaller differences in subjective than in performance-based assessments. Additionally, we find that contextual moderators, including leadership position, male-dominated industry, data collection year, participant age, and geographical region, are associated with the presence, magnitude, and direction of gender differences, suggesting that gender differences in EI vary across contexts. Overall, these findings show that women hold advantages in many emotional abilities, but that gender differences in EI are contingent on the target of emotional abilities, measurement type, and context, informing future research and theory building. author: Gaete, Jorge and Ríos, Natalia and Rojas-Barahona, Cristian A. and Salgado, Gabriel and Ramírez, Saray and Araya, Ricardo
title: Japi 2.0, a gaming platform to stimulate cognitive and socio-emotional skills in early childhood: results of a pilot randomized controlled trial
journal: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health
abstract: Background: Early childhood is a sensitive developmental period for the acquisition of cognitive and socio-emotional skills that are strongly associated with later mental health, academic achievement, and social functioning. Children growing up in socioeconomically disadvantaged contexts are at increased risk for early emotional and behavioral difficulties, highlighting the need for accessible, scalable, and developmentally appropriate preventive interventions. Japi 2.0 is a tablet-based gaming platform designed to stimulate six interrelated cognitive and socio-emotional skills—working memory, inhibitory control, emotion recognition, social competence, empathy, and cognitive planning—through structured play in preschool settings. Methods: We conducted a pilot cluster randomized controlled trial in low-income preschools in Santiago, Chile. Schools were randomized to either the Japi 2.0 intervention or treatment as usual. The intervention consisted of 24 individual sessions delivered over 12 weeks during regular class hours. Primary outcomes were acceptability (perceived by children, early years educators, and parents) and feasibility (recruitment, retention, attendance, intervention delivery, and data completeness). Secondary outcomes explored preliminary changes in cognitive, socio-emotional, and behavioral functioning using standardized assessments and parent- and teacher-reported measures. Exploratory analyses were conducted using multilevel models adjusted for baseline scores and clustering, based on available outcome data from randomized participants. Results: Japi 2.0 showed high acceptability across stakeholders. Educators and parents reported that the game and the accompanying web-based dashboard were engaging, age-appropriate, easy to use, and pedagogically relevant. Children reported high levels of enjoyment and positive emotional experiences during gameplay. Feasibility indicators were satisfactory: most planned sessions were delivered as scheduled, attendance was high, and outcome data completeness was adequate. Exploratory analyses indicated improvements over time in both groups across most outcomes. Preliminary exploratory signals favoring the intervention were observed for empathy and parent-reported emotional and behavioral difficulties; however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small number of clusters and exploratory nature of the analyses. Conclusions: This pilot trial demonstrates that Japi 2.0 is a feasible and highly acceptable digital intervention for preschool children in low-income educational settings. Although efficacy findings are preliminary, results support progression to a fully powered randomized controlled trial to evaluate effectiveness and longer-term impacts on cognitive, socio-emotional, and behavioral development. Trial registration Clinical Trials NCT06420544, May 20th, 2024. https://www.clinicaltrials.gov/study/ NCT06420544. © The Author(s) 2026.

author: van den Hee, Sarah M. and van Hooft, Edwin A. J. and Van Hoye, Greet and Nevicka, Barbara
title: Unemployment in later life: The effects of a job search skills training intervention and development orientations on job search and reemployment of older job seekers.
abstract: Late-career unemployment has a demonstrated negative impact on individuals and society. Yet little is known about the mechanisms through which policy programs operate to support older unemployed individuals in finding reemployment. The present study aimed to provide more insight into how a job search skills training program facilitates older job seekers in their reemployment process and who benefits most from the program. Using a two-group field experimental design among 4,625 unemployed job seekers aged over 50, we examined the effects of the job search skills training intervention on participants’ job search knowledge and self-efficacy, job search behaviors, and reemployment status and speed. In addition, the study examined whether the effects of job search skills training on job search knowledge and self-efficacy depend on older job seekers’ development orientations (i.e., future time perspective and learning goal orientation). Job search skills training was found to increase older job seekers’ job search knowledge and self-efficacy, and in turn their job search process quality, which then enhanced their chances and speed of finding reemployment. The positive effects of job search skills training on job search knowledge and self-efficacy appeared to be stronger for older job seekers with lower development orientations. The current findings advance training and job search theory by uncovering the explanatory mechanisms of a job search skills training program and by showing that individual attributes influence learning outcomes. Our findings also have important implications for the design, implementation, and evaluation of future policy programs aimed at older unemployed individuals and career counseling practice. author: Lievens, Filip and Zhou, You and Ng, Jomel Wei Xuan and Xi, Liyan and Tian, Yixin and Sackett, Paul R. and Martin-Raugh, Michelle
title: A meta-analytic examination of the criterion-related validity and cognitive loading associated with traditional and new situational judgment test paradigms.
abstract: Traditionally, situational judgment tests (SJTs) include text-based situations and ask candidates to pick the best and worst response option. Over the years, various new SJT paradigms have been developed to increase validity, reduce incidental cognitive load, and/or lower costs. Examples are multimedia SJTs, constructed response SJTs, and single-response SJTs. First, this study investigates how the traditional SJT paradigm performs in terms of criterion-related validity by updating prior meta-analyses. Second, this study provides initial, meta-analytic evidence on the criterion-related validity and cognitive load of several new SJT paradigms. On the basis of 457 independent samples from 302 studies (total N = 244,257), results showed that SJTs were not only predictive of job performance but also of academic performance, organizational citizenship behavior, and counterproductive work behavior. SJT validity was higher in operational (i.e., applicant) settings than in nonoperational settings and could also be expanded to new content (e.g., emotion and cross-cultural management). In terms of comparing traditional and new SJT paradigms, multimedia SJTs had validity equal to text-based ones but lower cognitive load. Importantly, the multiple-choice modality did not significantly outperform written constructed response modalities in terms of validity, and the cognitive loading of webcam-constructed responses was even lower than that of other response modalities. The implications of these findings are among others discussed in the context of the cost effectiveness of SJTs vis-à-vis other selection procedures. author: Feraco, Tommaso and Jach, Hayley K. and Bardach, Lisa and Kopatz, Myriel and Murayama, Kou and Sewell, Madison N. and Napolitano, Christopher M. and Soto, Christopher J.
title: Comparing change goals and feasibility beliefs about changing social, emotional, and behavioral skills vs. personality traits among adolescents, parents, and teachers
abstract: This study compared adolescents', parents', and teachers' change goals and feasibility beliefs for Big Five traits versus social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills. Participants were 676 Italian high school students who reported about themselves, 461 parents who reported about their participating child, and 704 international teachers reporting about students in general. We found that all groups viewed SEB skills as more changeable than traits, with the strongest skill preference among teachers. Student differences were clearest for Social Engagement versus Extraversion. Teachers, but not parents, also reported greater interest in skill-based than trait-based interventions. These findings suggest that skill framing may increase perceived malleability and support for developmental interventions in educational contexts. © 2026 The Authors

author: Wang, Faming and King, Ronnel B.
title: Students and schools have distinct configurations of socio-emotional skills: a multilevel latent profile analysis
abstract: Socio-emotional skills have attracted increasing attention due to their significance to students’ academic and well-being outcomes. However, there is ongoing debate in the literature over whether students’ socio-emotional skills vary quantitatively or qualitatively. Furthermore, existing research on these skills has primarily considered socio-emotional skills as individual attributes of students, with less attention devoted to the possibility that schools could also have distinct socio-emotional profiles. To address these gaps, this study employed a multilevel latent profile analysis to investigate profiles of socio-emotional skills at both student and school levels from a person-centered perspective. We also examined how these socio-emotional profiles are associated with school climates and academic and well-being outcomes. This study included 29,755 15-year-old students from nine countries. At the student level, we identified four distinct profiles that differed more in average skill levels: Low, Average, Moderately High, and High Socio-emotional Profiles. We also identified two types of schools: Lower Socio-emotional Schools and Higher Socio-emotional Schools. Positive school climates, characterized by high levels of school belonging, cooperation, positive teacher-student relationships, and a lower frequency of bullying, were associated with more adaptive socio-emotional profiles. Concerningly, only a small proportion of students (5%) and schools (28%) showed adaptive socio-emotional skills. Our findings suggest the need to implement targeted interventions to foster socio-emotional skills tailored to the needs of different subgroups. © The Author(s) 2026.

author: Mallin, Emily L. and Silva, Karina and Amarneh, Dania Y. and Cotton, Mallory R. and Hernandez Ortiz, Jessica and Trent, Erika S. and Zvolensky, Michael J. and Viana, Andres G.
title: Acculturative stress and internalizing problems among Latinos who drink hazardously: The roles of distress tolerance and emotion dysregulation.
abstract: Although acculturative stress contributes significantly to internalizing problems among Latinos who drink hazardously, the individual difference variables that strengthen or weaken this relationship have remained elusive. To address this gap, we examined two cognitive–affective factors, namely, distress tolerance and emotion dysregulation, as candidate moderators. We expected that acculturative stress would be positively associated with internalizing problems (operationalized as anxious arousal, traumatic intrusions, and social anxiety) at lower levels of distress tolerance and/or higher levels of emotion dysregulation. A sample of Latinos who drink hazardously (N = 99) completed measures of acculturative stress, distress tolerance, emotion dysregulation, and internalizing symptoms. There was a significant Acculturative Stress × Distress Tolerance interaction explaining 5.02% and 4.19% of the variance in anxious arousal and traumatic intrusions, respectively. Acculturative stress was significantly positively associated with anxious arousal and traumatic intrusions only at lower levels of distress tolerance. There was also a significant Acculturative Stress × Emotion Dysregulation interaction explaining 7.46% of the variance in anxious arousal. Acculturative stress was significantly positively associated with anxious arousal only at higher levels of emotion dysregulation. Acculturative stress was associated with anxious arousal and traumatic intrusions among Latinos who drink hazardously with lower distress tolerance and/or higher emotion dysregulation. Enhancing distress tolerance and lowering emotion dysregulation may protect Latino individuals who engage in hazardous drinking and experience acculturative stress against internalizing problems, and these processes may serve as targets in future intervention programming. author: Lubczyk, Till and Bleidorn, Wiebke and Hopwood, Christopher J. and Kretzschmar, Andre
title: Cognitive Abilities, Personality, and Sustainable Attitudes and Behavior
abstract: Climate change demands urgent action, yet individual engagement in sustainable behaviors remains inconsistent. We conducted two studies (N1 = 280, N2 = 973) examining how political orientation, personality traits, reasoning ability, social-emotional-behavioral skills, and complex problem solving relate to sustainable attitudes and behaviors in U.S. adults. Using structural equation modeling, we found that openness to experience was the strongest predictor, alongside liberal political orientation and self-perceived social engagement and innovation skills. Unexpectedly, both cognitive personality traits showed negative associations with sustainability outcomes, challenging the notion that cognitive abilities universally facilitate adaptive behavior. For sustainable behavior, these associations were small to moderate (-.25 <= r <= -.15) and most pronounced for food-related and engagement-related behaviors. Specification curve analyses confirmed that less established constructs (social, emotional, and behavioral skill self-concepts and complex problem solving) contributed meaningful variance beyond established personality predictors and that these associations were robust across analytical specifications. Overall, psychological characteristics together explained up to 44\\% of variance in sustainable attitudes and 29\\% of variance in sustainable behavior. These findings advance our understanding of the psychological underpinnings of environmental engagement and highlight the need for future research to clarify the mechanisms underlying the negative cognitive ability-sustainability association.

author: Santos., Amanda Espagolla and Melo-Silva., Lucy Leal and Oliveira., Jose Egidio Barbosa
title: What Drives Career Engagement? The Predictive Role of Socioemotional Skills and Career Adaptability
abstract: In contemporary labour markets characterized by uncertainty and rapid change, psychological resources that support proactive career behaviour are increasingly important. Drawing on Career Construction Theory, this study examined the relationships between socioemotional skills, career adaptability, and career engagement among university students. Participants were 204 interns who completed measures of socioemotional skills, career adaptability, and career engagement. Correlational analyses revealed positive associations among all major variables. Hierarchical regression showed that socioemotional skills significantly predicted career engagement after controlling for sociodemographic factors (Delta R \\& sup2; = .31, p < .001). However, the inclusion of career adaptability substantially increased explained variance (Delta R \\& sup2; = .26), with the final model accounting for 59.6\\% of the variance in engagement. Concern (beta = .301, p < .001), Confidence (beta = .204, p = .018), and Curiosity (beta = .193, p = .030) emerged as the strongest predictors. These findings suggest that while socioemotional skills provide a foundational basis, career adaptability represents a more proximal predictor of proactive career behaviour. The study contributes to the literature by clarifying the complementary roles of these constructs in fostering career engagement among university students.
